title: The table and the tablecloth today
word: The table and the tablecloth today
hook: Karo's code with Isserles' notes, still the reference rabbis reach for

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Tur, and your line: four rows. Prayer, food, family, money. Which row did you give a little more care? Day one thousand one hundred fourteen.

A code of law that begins in bed. Its first ruling is about waking up: a person should rise like a lion in the morning to serve the Creator, and be the one who wakes the dawn. Not the dawn waking you. You waking it. That's the opening of a book written by Rabbi Joseph Karo. And right there on the same page, set off from his words, a second rabbi adds a line before Karo's lion even gets out of bed. A verse from the Psalms: "I have set the LORD always before me." Two voices, one page, and the page is still open on desks today. Today's word is that pair.
screen: `RISE LIKE A LION.` → `A SECOND VOICE ON THE PAGE.` → `I HAVE SET THE LORD ALWAYS BEFORE ME.`

segments.voice: Karo called his code the Shulchan Arukh, the set table. The idea: the law laid out and ready, like a meal with every dish in its place. He had already written a long commentary weighing the earlier authorities, and this was its short, usable form, in brief rulings, following yesterday's four rows: prayer, food, family, money. Second, the tablecloth. In Poland, Rabbi Moses Isserles, known as the Rema, read the set table and saw that in places it didn't match the practice of his own Ashkenazi communities, since Karo had leaned on Sephardi authorities. So he didn't write a rival book. He wrote notes, and he called them the Mappah, the tablecloth, spread over Karo's table. Third, the page. The two are printed together, Karo's ruling and then, set off, the Rema's gloss. Where the two differ, Sephardi communities generally look to Karo and Ashkenazi communities to the Rema. Two traditions, sharing one table. Fourth, today. The Shulchan Arukh is printed surrounded by commentaries, and a rabbi answering an everyday question about Shabbat, a kosher kitchen or a business dispute may well start there. Over time the table has collected many guests, all arguing politely around the edges. But open it, and it still begins the same way. Rise like a lion. And above it, the Rema's line: "I have set the LORD always before me." Still the table.
screen: `THE SET TABLE: LAW, READY TO USE.` · `THE TABLECLOTH: ASHKENAZI PRACTICE.` · `TWO TRADITIONS ON ONE PAGE.` · `STILL WHERE THE QUESTION STARTS.` · then, large: `STILL THE TABLE.`

segments.voice: Today's practice begins with one everyday question. Settle, and let your breath slow. Choose a question from your own ordinary day. How to begin the morning. What to say before eating. How soon to pay someone who works for you. Don't look it up yet. Just hold the question, and notice how ordinary it is, and that a whole tradition thought it worth an answer. Later today, if you like, look it up in a guide to Jewish practice, or ask someone who keeps it. For now, sit with the question. The bell holds the time.
The table and the tablecloth. Karo's Shulchan Arukh, the set table, with the Rema's notes, the tablecloth, printed together on one page. Today's word.
screen: `THE TABLE AND THE TABLECLOTH — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: still the table. Tomorrow morning, try Karo's opening once: get up a moment before you have to, and wake the dawn instead of letting it wake you. Day one thousand one hundred fourteen.

howItsDone: Rabbis and students consult the Shulchan Arukh, printed with the Rema's glosses and later commentaries, when answering questions of daily practice; it is also a core text for those studying toward rabbinic ordination.
